client: It's been six months since my mom passed away, and I just can't seem to move forward like everyone else. My friends keep telling me I should be "getting better" by now, but I still cry every day when I'm alone. I don't even want to see them anymore because they act like everything's normal when my whole world fell apart.
therapist: You sound deeply pained and almost overwhelmed by grief—your voice carries so much sorrow and intensity when you talk about your mom. It makes sense that you'd feel isolated when others don’t seem to understand how raw this still is for you. Would it help to explore what "moving forward" would even look like for *you*, rather than what others expect?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess moving forward for me would mean being able to think about her without crying instantly. But I don't know if I even want that - it feels like if the pain fades, I'm forgetting her somehow. Everyone keeps saying time heals, but what if this is just how I am now?
therapist: I hear the conflict in your voice—part of you fears that healing might mean losing your connection to her, and that thought alone is heartbreaking. It’s okay if grief doesn’t follow a timeline; what if honoring her could coexist with moments of peace, not just pain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it that way - that I could miss her and still find peace sometimes. It just feels wrong when I have a good day, like I'm betraying her memory. But maybe... maybe she wouldn't want me to hurt like this forever.
therapist: You're speaking so gently about this—I can hear how much you're wrestling with guilt when moments of relief come. What if, instead of betrayal, those good days could be a quiet way of carrying her love forward?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That’s a really beautiful thought, but it’s hard to believe it right now. I keep thinking about all the things I didn’t do or say when she was here—all the regrets. It’s like those memories overshadow everything else, and I can’t imagine feeling okay without her.
therapist: Your voice carries such a mix of longing and pain when you talk about those regrets—it’s clear how much you wish things could have been different. It might help to gently ask yourself: would your mom want those regrets to define your memories of her, or would she want you to focus on the love you shared?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know she wouldn't want me to dwell on the regrets...she was always so forgiving. But that just makes me miss her more, you know? It's like the kinder I remember her being, the worse I feel for not appreciating it enough back then.
therapist: I hear how much this hurts—your voice speeds up and rises when you talk about her kindness, almost like the love feels overwhelming right now because you miss her so deeply. It might help to remember that grief isn’t just about regret; it’s also a reflection of how much her love mattered to you. Could we try holding space for both the pain *and* the gratitude?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to try holding space for both, but it's like my brain only wants to focus on what I lost. Maybe if I wrote her a letter? Though that seems silly since she's gone...but I don't know how else to sort through these feelings.
therapist: I can hear how torn you feel—your voice tightens when you mention writing the letter, like part of you wants to reach out but worries it won’t matter. It’s not silly at all; putting these feelings into words could help you untangle what’s weighing heaviest. Would you want to explore what you’d say in that letter without judging whether it’s "right"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I'd probably start with telling her how sorry I am for all the times I was too busy to call...but then I get stuck. Wouldn't it just be me listing all my failures? That doesn't seem very healing. Maybe this letter idea isn't such a good plan after all.
therapist: Your voice sounds so heavy when you talk about those missed calls—I can hear how much this particular regret weighs on your heart. What if the letter wasn’t about listing failures, but about telling her the things you’d want her to know now—not just the apologies, but the love behind them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about writing the love parts too...that actually makes my chest feel a little lighter. But what if I cry the whole time I'm writing? It feels like such a mess of emotions, I don't know if I can handle it.
therapist: It’s okay if you cry—your voice trembles as you talk about this, and it’s clear how deeply this touches your heart. Writing through tears can be healing, and it doesn’t have to happen all at once; you can take it step by step, letting the emotions flow as they come.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I could try writing a little at a time—maybe just a sentence or two to start. But I’m scared it’ll make me feel worse, like opening a floodgate I can’t close. What if I just end up crying for hours and can’t stop?
therapist: Your voice sounds shaky and hurried—it’s clear this idea brings up a lot of fear and uncertainty for you. What if we thought of this as opening the floodgate just a crack at a time? You don’t have to dive into everything all at once; even a sentence or two can be a gentle way to start honoring your feelings.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Okay...maybe I'll try writing just one thing I miss about her tonight. But what if I can't stop at just one? I know myself - once I start remembering, it all comes rushing back and I can't think about anything else for days.
therapist: I hear how scared you are of being overwhelmed—your voice speeds up and climbs higher when you talk about the memories rushing back, like you’re bracing for a wave. What if we set a simple limit, like writing for just five minutes and then doing something grounding afterward? That way, you can honor the grief *and* protect yourself from feeling lost in it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
